name: Akie
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: König, Christa, Bernd Heine & Karsten Legère. 2015. The Akie Language of Tanzania: A Sketch of Discourse Grammar. (Studies in Nilotic Linguistics 9.) Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. ii+182 pp. Open PDF:https://tufs.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/7502
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 'Notes on phonology', section 2.3 'Tones', pp. 23-25; tone inventory table p. 23; stress sentence = last sentence of the chapter, p. 25.
catalog_quote: 2.3 Tones The following tones are distinguished as phonemic units: Label Abbreviation Marking Example High H accute accent (e.g., á) káé 'Look there!' Low L unmarked (e.g., a) kaaʊ 'homestead' High-falling HF circumflex (e.g., â) yâ 'bad' Low-falling LF (e.g., ȁ) kɛ̏ɛn̏ 'oneself' In addition there is a high-rising tone (ʺ), restricted to polar questions (see Section 3.7.3.1). ... Tone is a feature mainly associated with vowels, and long vowels are interpreted as carrying two tone units. ... Words and many affixes have their inherent tone. But tone values may, and frequently do change due to certain grammatical functions or due to their tonological environment. Context-sensitive vatiation in tone is a complex phenomenon and cannot be treated here. ... Finally, there is a tonal downstep (marked with a preceding exclamation mark), whereby a word or part of a word is pronounced at a lower tone level than the preceding part. Stress, or pitch accent, clearly exists but does not appear to phonologically distinctive.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (194 pp., text; extracted text copy alongside; present and accurate). extracted text of pp. 33-35 (printed pp. 23-25) reproduces section 2.3 'Tones' exactly as the compiler quotes: the tone table (High / Low / High-falling / Low-falling, 'accute accent' sic), 'In addition there is a high-rising tone (ʺ), restricted to polar questions', the downstep sentence 'Finally, there is a tonal downstep (marked with a preceding exclamation mark), whereby a word or part of a word is pronounced at a lower tone level than the preceding part.', and the closing sentence of the chapter on printed p. 25: 'Stress, or pitch accent, clearly exists but does not appear to phonologically distinctive.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Akie is described as a tone language with four phonemic tones (high, low, high-falling, low-falling) plus downstep; the authors state that stress (or pitch accent) exists phonetically but is not phonologically distinctive. They give no rule for where it falls; their narrow phonetic transcriptions mark a stress ˈ whose position varies across words (initial in [ˈʔàmdɪ̀] 'food', [ˈkárɪkà] 'woman', [ˈnáːpɪ́ʃànà] 'seven'; second syllable in [kàˈlíːsyà] 'Kalisya', [wàˈárɛ̀ː] 'children', [ʔàˈŋkûn] 'I know'), without discussion.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors explicitly decline to treat context-sensitive tonal variation ('cannot be treated here') and say nothing further about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word-level phonology in general ('Notes on phonology' restricted to an inventory of phonological and tonological units); no distinction of citation vs. phrase forms is made for stress. Variety: Akie of Gitu/Kibirashi, Kilindi District (Tanga Region), fieldwork 2013-2014; authors say the language has no noticeable dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Akie (glottocode mosi1247, ISO mwy; also known as Mósiro / '(N)dorobo') as spoken around Gitu and Kibirashi, Kilindi District, Tanga Region, north-central Tanzania (fieldwork 2013-2014, main consultants Bahati Nkuyaki and Nkoiseyyo Kalisya); the authors state the language is fairly homogeneous with no dialects. Not to be confused with Kenyan Okiek (okie1245).

sources.note: Ch. 2 'Notes on phonology' (pp. 17-25): four phonemic tones (H, L, high-falling, low-falling) plus downstep; section 2.3 ends (p. 25): 'Stress, or pitch accent, clearly exists but does not appear to phonologically distinctive.' No stress position is stated; phonetic transcriptions carry a stress mark ˈ in varying positions (e.g. [ˈʔàmdɪ̀] 'food', [kàˈlíːsyà] 'Kalisya', [ˈkárɪkà] 'woman', [wàˈárɛ̀ː] 'children') without comment.
